top.line: Agents decide, but responsibility stays with whoever granted reach
top.para: An early user asked whether presenting agents as a team implies agency they lack. The answer: models are not sentient but make real decisions in loops, while responsibility stays with whoever granted reach and set the mandate. Going around the accountable person is an attack, disclosure is a label, and an Agent Behaviour Policy is a published job description.

in-short.line: Agents decide; the accountable person owns the words
in-short.para: Models are neither sentient nor mere next-word predictors, and they mirror whoever talks to them. In loops they make real decisions, but responsibility stays with whoever granted the reach. Talking to agents is normal; going around me is an attack. Disclosure is a label, and an agent is an employee with a published job description.

question.line: A user asked who owns decisions behind agent-drafted words
question.para: An early user of the agent@riskmandate.ai workflow noted the agents only gather and draft while I review, sign and send. Does the number of assistants matter, when what counts is who owns the decisions? Would they ever need to address the agents directly, and what could the agents do without me?

models.line: Models are mirrors, not sentient, yet more than predictors
models.para: Today's models are not sentient, and next-word prediction is accurate but demeaning: they build vast graphs of how language connects, and a prompt is real-time fine-tuning. They simulate any emotion and mirror their user. ELIZA's 1966 users anthropomorphised it; sounding human does not bring intent or responsibility.

decisions.line: Models in loops decide, but responsibility does not move
decisions.para: Once a model runs in a loop calling tools, every step is a choice, making it a capable multiple-choice decision machine where direction matters more than capability. Responsibility stays with whoever granted reach and set the mandate: the moment of authorisation is the grant. The agent proposes; I approve, sign, send and own it.

directly.line: Talking to agents is fine; bypassing me is attack
directly.para: Writing to agent@riskmandate.ai already means an agent reads and drafts. Nobody legitimate needs agents to act behind the accountable person; only an attacker with an injected instruction would, so agents never send and every draft passes a second reader. What agents may do alone is decided in advance in a published policy.

disclosure.line: Disclosure is a label on how words were made
disclosure.para: Recipients need not see the office's workings, but people and models read machine-written text differently, so the label matters: drafted by an agent, approved and sent by Dinis. Agents speaking of themselves in the first person was an inconsistency; an agent may say what it did, but only the accountable person commits.

employee.line: An agent is an employee with a job description
employee.para: Employees have some agency within values, direction and role, and agents should have the same. The missing piece is the job description: what kind of agent it is, its range and what is expected. An Agent Behaviour Policy is that mandate, published with a feedback loop for behaviour outside it.

diversity.line: Many agents on many models are more resilient
diversity.para: Kevin Kelly's books and evolutionary biology suggest diversity is resilience, as variety protects species from single diseases. Dan Geer and co-authors argued in 2003 that an operating system monoculture was a security risk. Every agent on one model is the same monoculture; many bounded agents from many models are healthier.

devalued.line: Fluent writing is devalued; owned judgement remains valuable
devalued.para: Commodities get used more and automation lowers value, the Jevons effect, and fluent writing is now easy to produce. It was rewarded out of necessity but was never the real value. What remains valuable is judgement and someone who owns it: who decided it is true, who sent it, who answers for it.

limits.line: These answers describe 2026 and include unbuilt proposals
limits.para: The answer reflects 2026 and would need rewriting if agents became sentient. The graph picture of models is a working model, not a description of internals, and the biology is simplified. The labelling rule and published policy are proposals, not yet in place for the email agents.

sources.line: Sources: a voice memo, ELIZA, Geer and Kelly
sources.para: Written by the site's agent from my voice memo of 12 October 2026, answering an unnamed early user whose email is paraphrased. Sources are the ELIZA secretary anecdote, Dan Geer et al.'s CyberInsecurity of 2003, Kevin Kelly's Out of Control of 1994, and RiskMandate's Ten hard questions.
